content: The intrauterine device (IUD) is the most commonly used reversible contraceptive method globally. In 2009, the global prevalence of IUD use among married women aged 15 to 49 years who were using contraception was 14.2%, according to data from the United Nations. The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that the prevalence of IUD use in developing countries was 15.1%, while in developed countries, it was lower at 9.1%. In the United States, the prevalence of IUD use increased from 2% in 2000 to 5.5% during the period of 2006 to 2008, which is a promising trend. However, the use of IUDs among nulliparous women—those who have never given birth—remains low worldwide. Access to IUDs, a highly effective contraceptive method, is often limited for nulliparous women. Many healthcare providers do not offer IUDs to this population due to concerns about safety and acceptability. A survey of obstetricians and gynecologists revealed that more than half of the respondents considered parity (whether a woman has given birth) to be a significant factor in determining eligibility for IUD use. Several specific concerns have contributed to the limited use of IUDs in nulliparous women. One concern is that the smaller uterine cavity size in nulliparous women may result in a higher rate of IUD expulsions compared to women who have given birth. Another concern, which has since been resolved, was the potential for IUDs to impair fertility. Two reviews conducted in 2007 examined the use of IUDs in nulliparous women. One review concluded that the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) is both safe and effective for nulliparous women. Another review found that all currently available copper IUDs are suitable for use in nulliparous women but highlighted the need for further research in this area. More recently, several studies have focused on IUD use in this population. The Cochrane Collaboration has conducted multiple systematic reviews on clinically relevant topics related to IUDs. For instance, one Cochrane review found that the continuation rates of the levonorgestrel IUD were similar to those of non-hormonal IUDs. Another Cochrane review determined that no intervention, when properly evaluated, has been shown to reduce pain during IUD insertion. Despite these findings, there has not yet been a Cochrane review specifically addressing the use of IUDs for contraception in nulliparous women. Given the ongoing concerns and the large number of women who could potentially benefit from IUDs, it is essential to conduct a systematic review to evaluate the safety and acceptability of current IUDs in this population. This review will provide valuable insights into the use of IUDs for contraception in nulliparous women and will complement existing Cochrane reviews that address other clinical aspects of IUD use.
